references.text: Two men went up to the temple to pray. The temple was the central place of prayer in Israel, as Solomon requested at its dedication ([ref:1 Kings 8:30|1 Kings 8:30]).
To "go up" to the temple was a common expression, since the temple was located on a hill in Jerusalem ([ref:Psalms 122:1|Psalms 122:1]).
The temple is called a house of prayer for all peoples, which highlights its function as a place of prayer ([ref:Isaiah 56:7|Isaiah 56:7]).

The Pharisees and the scribes criticized Jesus for eating with tax collectors and sinners. This contrast between Pharisees and tax collectors is a recurring theme in the Gospel of Luke ([ref:Luke 5:30|Luke 5:30]).

Tax collectors acknowledged God's righteousness by being baptized, while the Pharisees rejected God's plan – a contrast that mirrors the parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector ([ref:Luke 7:29-30|Luke 7:29-30]).

Jesus welcomed tax collectors and sinners, which the Pharisees grumbled about. This tension between the self-righteous and the humble forms the background for the parable ([ref:Luke 15:1-2|Luke 15:1-2]).

Jesus said that tax collectors and prostitutes would enter God's kingdom before the religious leaders, reflecting the same theme that the despised win God's favor over the self-righteous ([ref:Matthew 21:31-32|Matthew 21:31-32]).
Peter and John went up to the temple at the hour of prayer, showing that the temple was still used as a place of prayer by believers ([ref:Acts 3:1|Acts 3:1]).
Jesus cleansed the temple and declared it should be a house of prayer, emphasizing the temple as the place where the two men in the parable went to pray ([ref:Luke 19:46|Luke 19:46]).
